justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level of the underlying asset at the time of the forecast, which I assumed was trading near the 395–397 range. For the 1-day horizon, I applied minimal drift, essentially expecting the price to stay close to its current level with only ordinary intraday noise factored in, producing a point estimate of 396.5. For the 1-week horizon, I built in a slight upward bias of roughly 2–3 dollars, reflecting a modest positive momentum assumption and the tendency for markets to drift modestly when there is no strong directional signal. For the 1-month horizon, I extended that drift assumption further to 405, which represents an annualized gain in the low-to-mid single digits — a reasonable baseline for an equity index or similar instrument in a neutral-to-slightly-bullish environment.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using typical realized volatility at each time horizon. For the 1-day interval, I used a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus 11–12 dollars, consistent with daily volatility in the 1.5–2% range. For the 1-week interval, I widened the band to about plus or minus 23 dollars, scaling by the square root of time in a standard fashion. The 1-month interval is considerably wider at plus or minus 50 dollars, reflecting not only the accumulation of daily variance over roughly 22 trading days but also the increased probability of regime changes, macro surprises, or shifts in market sentiment over a longer window.

The most significant risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic data shocks — such as an unexpected inflation print, a central bank policy surprise, or a sharp deterioration in labor market data — any of which could produce a multi-percent move within a single session. Geopolitical events, credit market stress, or a liquidity crunch could similarly produce outsized moves. On the upside, a strongly positive earnings surprise season or a dovish pivot from a major central bank could push prices well above 455 on the 1-month horizon. These tail risks are inherently difficult to quantify and represent the primary reason why even the 90% confidence intervals may understate true uncertainty during periods of elevated macro tension.
